cards.title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2

depth.text: someone broke out of a **Firecracker virtual machine** and made its host run code as **root**

They traced a **guest memory page** back to the host process, then changed the live vCPU thread’s **saved registers** so Firecracker called its write wrapper when it returned from KVM. A **serial-port write** triggered the call; this test had no jailer, while production containment can drop privileges and restrict Firecracker through namespaces and seccomp.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says the write-up is informative; another calls it “pure LLM slop.”

comments.text: I really wish they would have expanded on this paragraph in their article further: > The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. A deployment using those controls requires a separate assessment of the privileges and resources available after compromising its VMM. If I'm…

I am more convinced by the day that the Nova Microhypervisor approach is correct. Do virtualization with a tiny formally verified microkernel and have complex kernels like Linux run underneath instead of letting a huge, complex, and brittle linux kernel and vm ecosystem control the hypervisor layer. https://hypervisor.org/

I have a demo service that entirely relies on Firecracker VMs: ClickBench playground, https://benchmark.clickhouse.com/playground/ It hosts hundreds of database engines - many of them have vulnerabilities, and some of them, like Pandas, are basically open RCEs regardless. We can PoC the Firecracker VM Escape on that service.

This is not a new vulnerability, it's just a description of how to exploit the PwnEscape vulnerability in practice on firecracker VMs (disclosed multiple weeks ago and discussed in some less upvoted posts on HN)

glossary.ABI: Application Binary Interface: the agreed rules software uses to communicate with other software.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.opaque handle: A reference you can use to work with something without seeing how it is built inside.
glossary.TUI: Terminal User Interface: the menus and controls an app shows inside a text terminal.
glossary.identity resolution: Matching records from different sources so they point to the right real person.
glossary.over-merging: Combining records from different people as if they belonged to one person.
glossary.confidence calibration: How well a model’s confidence scores match how often it is actually right.
glossary.decision model: A program that weighs possible choices and predicts or selects one.
glossary.hybrid model: A setup that uses one model first and sends selected cases to another for review.
glossary.MS-DOS: Microsoft Disk Operating System: older computer software that runs programs using typed commands.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.S-1: A filing that gives investors details about a company's finances and share offering before an IPO.
glossary.lockup schedule: A timetable showing when certain shareholders are allowed to sell their shares.
glossary.Dutch auction: A way to set a sale price from buyers’ bids instead of choosing one fixed price first.
glossary.LPs: Limited partners: investors who put money into a fund run by someone else.
glossary.inference: When an AI uses what it learned to answer or act, instead of being trained.
glossary.commoditized: When something becomes easy to swap for similar options, so sellers struggle to stand out.
glossary.capabilities progress: How quickly AI systems get better at the abilities being measured.
glossary.compute multiplier: An improvement that lets the same amount of computer power get more AI progress.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.model weights: The learned settings inside an AI that shape how it responds.
glossary.alignment: The effort to keep an AI's actions in line with what people want.
glossary.compounding acceleration: When each improvement helps bring about further improvements, making progress speed up again.
glossary.bare-metal programming: Writing software for a computer to run without a normal operating system in between.
glossary.UEFI: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface: the built-in startup software that checks a computer and starts its main software.
glossary.linking: Joining compiled pieces of a program so they can run together.
glossary.EFI system partition: A section of a disk where a computer keeps files it needs to start up.
glossary.external symbols: Names of functions that a program expects to find in other code.
glossary.bootloader: A small program that starts a computer and loads its main software.
glossary.microVM: A small, separate computer environment for running a job; here, it gets thrown away when the job ends.
glossary.vCPU: Virtual CPU: a processor assigned to a virtual machine.
glossary.KVM: Kernel-based Virtual Machine: a Linux feature for running virtual machines.
glossary.EPT: Extended Page Tables: tables that translate a virtual machine’s memory addresses into locations in the host machine’s memory.
glossary.pt_regs: A record of the CPU’s saved state, including where a program should resume.
glossary.ASLR: Address Space Layout Randomization: a way to move parts of a program around each time it runs, making some attacks harder.
glossary.jailer: A helper that starts Firecracker with limits on its permissions and access.
glossary.namespaces: A Linux feature that gives a process its own view of things like other processes or the network.
glossary.seccomp: A Linux control that limits which requests a program can make to the system’s core.
glossary.root: The highest level of control on a computer, with permission to change system settings and files.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.proposed repo: A place Ubuntu puts updates for testing before moving them into the regular updates.
glossary.QA: Quality assurance: checking that software works as expected before people rely on it.
glossary.kernel: A small program that carries out a calculation on a computer's graphics chip or processor.
glossary.LTS: Long-term support: a release its makers promise to support for an extended period.
glossary.mitigation: A step taken to make a problem less harmful or disruptive.
glossary.sodium-ion battery: A battery that uses sodium rather than lithium; this article discusses it for storing electricity.
glossary.LFP: Lithium iron phosphate: a type of rechargeable battery used here as a comparison for sodium-ion batteries.
glossary.cell-level cost parity: When the battery cells themselves cost about the same, before comparing the rest of a complete storage system.
glossary.GWh: Gigawatt-hours: a measure of an amount of electricity, often used to describe how much a battery can store.
glossary.total cost of ownership: The full cost of using something over its lifetime, not just what it costs to buy.
glossary.UI: User interface: the screens and controls people use to operate a device.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.headless: Software that another program can control without a person using its regular screen.
glossary.element tree: A nested outline of the parts that make up a screen, such as a label inside a window.
glossary.native UI: An app’s screens and controls built for a device’s own system.
glossary.feature flag: A switch developers can use to turn a feature on or off without removing it from the program.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
glossary.local evaluation: Checking a flag inside the application, rather than making a network call each time.
glossary.microplastics: Tiny pieces of plastic that can shed from products and end up in food or the environment.
glossary.compostable: Able to break down into material that can be used as compost.
glossary.brew path: The parts inside a coffee machine that hot water and coffee pass through.
